NOR REPUBLIC OF THE PHILIPPINES DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMEN DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA comer Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City www.dilg.gov.ph BIVAHENG PINOY UVANO UAUMAD DILG Legal Opinion No. 35, S. 2014 HON. NEIL L. MONTALLANA 2 0 NOV 2014 Sanggunian Bayan Member Municipality of Daraga, Province of Albay Dear Hon. Montallana: This has reference to your letter dated 18 September 2014 requesting this Department's legal opinion regarding the interpretation of the phrase person or committee" as used in Section 86 of Republic Act No. 7160 or the Local Government code (LGC) of 1991. In this regard, please be informed that the phrase "person or committee" as used in Section 86 of the LGC refers only to person/s or individual/s or group thereof who are employees of the local government unit, over which the Municipal Mayor, as the case may be, exercises administrative authority or disciplinary powers as Local Chief Executive. It stands to reason that the Local Chief Executive can only delegate a power or authority vested upon him to an individual or person who is under his authority. This is so because only acts of subordinates are subject to review by their superiors. In closing, a delegation of the power to conduct administrative investigation, based on Section 86 of the LGC may prove to be an undue delegation of power if done in favor of private persons or individuals who are not even public officers or employees under the power of the delegating authority. Governmental functions, like the power to conduct administrative investigations, may only be exercised by public officers or employees. "Neither the 1987 Constitution nor RA 6670 (The Ombudsman Act of 1989) defines who "public officers "are. Instead, its varied definitions and concepts are found in different statutes and jurisprudence. Usually quoted in our decisions is Mechem, a recognized authority on the subject. In the 2002 case of Laurel v. Desierto, the Court extensively quoted his exposition on the term "public officers": A public office is the right. authority and duty. created and conferred by law. by which. for a given period. either fixed by law or enduring at the pleasure of the creating power, an individual is invested with some portion fthe sov i n functio f the overnment to be exercis by him for the benefit of the public. The individual so invested is a public officer. The characteristics of a public office, according to Mechem, include the delegation of sovereign functions, its

creation by law and not by contract, an oath, salary, continuance of the position, scope OT duties, and the designation of the position as an office. xxx xxx xxx Mechem describes the delegation to the individual of the sovereign functions of government as "[t]he most important characteristic" in determining whether a position is a public office or not. The most important characteristic which distinguishes an office from an employment or contract is that the creation and conferring of an office involves a dele ation to the individua f some o the soverei functions of government to be exercised bv him for the benefit of the ublic• — that some rtion of the soverei nt of the country, either legislative. executive, or judicial. attaches, for the time being, to be exercised for the public benefit. Unless the powers conferred are of' this nature. the individual is not a public officer. (Italics supplied) From the foregoing, it can be reasonably inferred that "public officers" are those endowed with the exercise of sovereign executive, legislative or judicial functions. The explication of the term is also consistent with the Court's pronouncement in Quimpo that, in the case of officers/employees in GOCCs, they are deemed "public officers" if their corporations are tasked to carry out governmental functions.'" (Italics and underscoring supplied) Trusting that the foregoing provided enlightenment to your concern. Thank you. LIIs:25/11 DIR.
